title: How we cut the cost of Shor’s arithmetic for RSA-2048
excerpt: One quantum table lookup can serve several primes. At 1,806 logical qubits, that idea helped us cut the estimated Toffoli count by 46%.
text: One quantum table lookup can serve several primes. At 1,806 logical qubits, that idea helped us cut the estimated Toffoli count by 46%. !RSA-2048 runtime versus physical qubits. Four blue stars show our surface-code, neutral-atom, Pinnacle 1.0 and cat-qubit estimates. The table pairs each with its reference.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1Y9-3xwWnnOX2HfFEwDqWw.png The stars mark four conditional hardware estimates using three circuits from our family. Each model uses its own timing, error and layout assumptions. The rows below the chart pair each scenario with the reference used in our paper. For cat qubits, varying the assumed overhead moves our estimate from 1.21 to 1.70 days, a range that includes the published two-engine estimate of 1.59 days. Imagine asking a database for the same row eight times, once for each column you need. You could ask for all eight columns in one query. A similar opportunity turned up in the quantum arithmetic used to factor RSA-2048. The circuit was repeatedly looking up the same address in different tables. We packed the answers together. We applied this idea to Craig Gidney’s 2025 construction for Shor’s algorithm in our paper, Shared Lookups and Lazy Residues. We also changed how the circuit stores and cleans up intermediate results. The goal was to lower the cost of the arithmetic that a fault-tolerant quantum computer would have to run. Gidney’s reference constructionhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917 One address, several answers Shor’s algorithm needs to work with powers of a number modulo the integer being factored. The reference circuit makes that arithmetic manageable by working with remainders modulo many small primes. Each prime has its own table, but in one costly stage, every table is addressed by the same chunk of exponent bits. A Toffoli gate flips a target qubit when its two controls are both 1. Toffolis are costly to implement in many error-corrected architectures, so they’re a useful unit for comparing circuits. In this construction, the Toffoli cost of the lookup itself is driven mainly by the number of possible addresses. The lookup can return a wider answer at roughly the same Toffoli cost. We put the entries for several primes side by side in each row and split the returned word into its pieces. The wider answer still takes extra workspace and has to be moved and used. We isolated this change in a matched comparison. With the same lookup window, register trimming, and checkpoint settings, sharing one lookup across three primes reduced the estimated Toffoli count by 28.8%. Keep the intermediate results and reduce once Quantum arithmetic has a cleanup bill. Temporary registers have to be returned to zero while preserving the computation’s output and relative phases. In one stage of the reference circuit, the cleanup recomputes intermediate remainders. We keep those remainders as checkpoints instead. That uses extra qubits and lets us subtract the same values we added on the way forward. Keeping the checkpoints also lets us postpone modular reduction. For example, 17 and 2 represent the same remainder modulo 5. If a register has room for the larger value, the circuit can carry it forward and reduce it when the next stage needs the usual remainder. These are our lazy residues. The paper proves that, under the stated register-width conditions, the changes preserve the reference output and its quantum phases. !Flow diagram of the reference arithmetic. Shared lookups target loop 1. Checkpoints and lazy residues target loop 3 and its cleanup.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/10mFCi6SI07PJjDUJ34HC1A.png From the paper. The reference circuit spends 55% of its Toffoli gates on the first lookup stage and 30% on cleaning up loop 3. The blue boxes show where the changes apply. What happens at the same qubit budget? Giving the reference circuit more qubits can also reduce its gate count. We evaluated its published cost model over 534,240 retained parameter settings and used the cheapest reference setting that fit each budget. We estimated the costs of our circuits with a benchmark built on the reference simulator. - 1,461 logical qubits. An estimated 5.08 billion Toffoli gates per factoring, down from 5.98 billion for the best reference setting in that budget. That’s a 15% reduction. - 1,806 logical qubits. An estimated 2.55 billion Toffoli gates per factoring, down from 4.74 billion. That’s a 46% reduction. Those figures count logical gates and include the expected cost of repeated shots. They come from resource estimates for RSA-2048. The paper reports sampling checks and validation on smaller circuits. !The new circuit frontier is below the reference curve at the highlighted budgets, saving 15 percent at 1,461 logical qubits and 46 percent at 1,806.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1V7lfYVDPfXBAdrWKwfpkbw.png From the paper. At a given logical qubit budget, the grey curve is the cheapest reference setting and the blue curve is the best circuit we benchmarked. The vertical gap shows the Toffoli savings. What would it take to run Shor’s algorithm on RSA-2048? The numbers above describe the circuit: how many error-protected logical qubits it needs and how many Toffoli gates it uses. A hardware estimate adds the physical qubits needed to encode those logical qubits, detect errors, and supply the resources for gates. It also estimates elapsed time from the device’s speed, how much work can run in parallel, and how often the circuit has to be repeated. These studies model a future machine running the full computation. None reports an RSA-2048 factorization performed on hardware. - Surface codes. Gidney and Ekerå estimated about 20 million physical qubits and eight hours in 2021. Gidney’s 2025 design estimated fewer than a million physical qubits and less than a week under the same basic hardware assumptions. The later circuit uses more Toffoli gates and fewer factories to supply them, trading time for a smaller machine. 2021 studyhttps://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2021-04-15-433/ · 2025 studyhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917 - Neutral atoms. Cain and colleagues model RSA-2048 designs with about 11,000–13,000 atoms whose runtimes stretch into decades. Their faster design projects 97 days with about 102,000 atoms by doing much more work in parallel. The models assume an error correction cycle of 1 millisecond. Cain et al.https://arxiv.org/html/2603.28627v1 - Pinnacle 1.2. Iceberg Quantum reports 72,000 physical qubits and 3.7 days at a 0.1% physical error rate and a 1 microsecond code cycle. At a tenfold lower error rate, its model gives 48,000 qubits and just under a day. These estimates combine a compiled circuit with simulated error correction. Pinnacle 1.2 releasehttps://www.iceberg-quantum.com/blog/releases/pinnacle-1-2/ - Superconducting cat qubits. Pappalardo and colleagues estimate 22,593 physical cat qubits and 3.14 days for their compiled layout, under a model with strongly suppressed bit flips. A more parallel layout in the same study uses about 611,000 cat qubits to bring the estimate down to 1.25 hours. Pappalardo et al.https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37839 A qubit count makes sense alongside the runtime, error model, and layout it comes with. The cat-qubit study makes this especially clear: the same team can estimate a run in hours or days by choosing how much hardware to devote to parallel work. The earlier stories in this series look at these hardware trade-offs in more detail. Quantum Factoring serieshttps://medium.com/@monitsharma/list/quantum-factoring-8d25eddc0b4d The hardware decides how much time you save A wide lookup is attractive when the processor can handle the output efficiently. On a space-efficient neutral-atom processor, the same output is expensive to deliver in pieces. These comparisons start from the same residue arithmetic, but each hardware model prices lookups and workspace differently. In our simplified surface-code allocation, the six-prime circuit takes 1.46 days at 1.33 million physical qubits. The reference in the same model takes 3.48 days at 0.98 million qubits. In Cain et al.’s balanced model, the two-prime circuit fits the published memory and takes an estimated 22.9 years versus 28.3 years for the tuned reference. On the space-efficient neutral-atom processor, the eight-prime circuit takes about 37% longer than the tuned reference, even with an assumed memory expansion. The neutral-atom architecture studyhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28627 !The eight-prime circuit takes 0.40 times the reference runtime in the surface-code model and 1.37 times in the compact neutral-atom model, which assumes extra memory.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1cmsVyF76Og3OjDW6tpEFmg.png From the paper. Each bar compares a circuit with the reference tuned for the same architecture. Below 1× is faster. Hatched bars assume additional memory whose physical cost was not estimated. We also estimate how the arithmetic might transfer to the published Pinnacle 1.0 and cat-qubit designs. In the Pinnacle 1.0 model, at a budget of 142,260 physical qubits, the eight-prime circuit takes an estimated 5.07 days versus 6.01 days for the best reference setting in the disclosed parameter and parallelism grid. This assumes the timing and error models still apply to a wider processing unit. Pinnacle 1.2 and Cain et al.’s 97-day design use their own circuits and hardware assumptions. A head-to-head hardware comparison would require compiling the circuits for the same machine and accounting for routing and retries on the same terms. Pinnacle 1.0 studyhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11457 What this paper is useful for If you’re designing a fault-tolerant machine, our circuits give you several ways to spend the same logical qubit budget. A processor with room for wide lookups can test larger groups of primes. A processor that moves small chunks of data can test smaller groups or keep checkpoints without sharing. The next step is to compile those choices for the target machine and measure how much time and workspace each needs. If you’re building resource estimates, the open benchmark lets you rerun the comparisons, tune the reference at the same qubit budget, and price the same arithmetic on another architecture. That gives people assessing the long-term risk to RSA a better input to their estimates: a smaller logical circuit whose hardware cost can be tested explicitly. Preprint on arXiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08907https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08907. The benchmark code, candidate circuits, and results are in the rsabench archive on Zenodohttps://zenodo.org/records/23991044. title: Peaked-Circuit Recovery on 98 Qubits
excerpt: Quantum hardware results, classical structural reduction, and verification of P11 and P12
text: Quantum hardware results, classical structural reduction, and verification of P11 and P12 !Project overview. Corrected Helios-1 shots lead to decoded answers. Classical structural reduction retains 284 of 1,999 units for P11 and 279 of 2,457 for P12. Both routes recover the same 98 bits for each circuit. The bottom strips encode the actual accepted answers.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1Crb6HZagzwflmkxtweBYQ.png Two approaches to the same P11 and P12 answers. The curves use recorded hardware shots, and the bars use the inferred classical core sizes. This study examines recovery of the accepted outputs of the 98-qubit P11 and P12 peaked circuits through quantum hardware measurements and classical circuit analysis. Quantinuum Helios-1 datasets containing 50 and 200 corrected shots yield the accepted strings under both weighted-medoid and cluster-consensus decoding. A subsequent structural classical method recovers the same outputs by identifying inverse-pair anchors, approximating the obfuscated middle by wire permutations, and contracting reduced models containing 284 and 279 two-qubit units. We report the recovered bitstrings, distinguish observed hardware frequencies from reduced-model probabilities, and examine the implications for verifiable quantum benchmarking. Introduction and research motivation P11 and P12 are public instances of the BlueQubit Peaked Portal challenge. Their objective is to recover a designated output string from a circuit whose ideal distribution concentrates probability on that string. This study compares two sources of information available to a solver, the distribution observed on quantum hardware and the structure retained in the published circuit description. Peaked circuits address a central difficulty in quantum-advantage experiments, efficient verification. For general quantum sampling tasks, evaluating the probabilities needed to assess an output distribution can itself require substantial classical computation. A circuit with a planted output of elevated probability offers a simpler verification procedure. A verifier that retains the target from circuit construction can check a submitted n-bit answer by direct comparison. The solver’s task is to recover that answer from the released circuit. Aaronson and Zhang introduced peaked-circuit sampling as a candidate approach to this verification problem. Aaronson and Zhang, 2024https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14493 Peak probability determines the sampling resources required. For independent samples from a fixed distribution with target probability p, the expected waiting time for its first occurrence is 1/p, and the probability of observing it within N samples is 1 − 1 − p^N. A target probability that scales as an inverse polynomial therefore permits polynomial sample complexity. Whether a particular construction achieves sufficient concentration while resisting classical recovery remains an empirical and theoretical question. These circuits also provide a system-level benchmark of state preparation, compiled circuit execution, measurement, and classical decoding. Successful recovery tests whether a recognisable computational signal survives the entire experimental workflow. Gharibyan and colleagues developed heuristic peaked-circuit constructions and demonstrated their use on Quantinuum H2. The P11 and P12 experiments considered here extend the study of recovery to the supplied 98-qubit challenge instances. Gharibyan et al., 2025https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25838 The benchmark’s scientific value also depends on sustained classical analysis. Kremer and Dupuis showed that mirrored structure and hidden permutations could be exploited to simulate earlier heuristic peaked circuits efficiently. Such results test the construction’s resistance to specialised algorithms and refine the classical baseline against which hardware performance is assessed. The P11/P12 structural method discussed below provides a further instance-specific example of this interaction between benchmark design and classical recovery. Kremer and Dupuis, 2026https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21908 A peaked circuit assigns unusually high ideal probability to a particular output string. For 98 qubits there are 2⁹⁸ possible strings. The mathematical target is a maximizer of the circuit’s output probability. Hardware measurements instead sample the distribution of the physical device’s final state. !The ideal probability p\Ux is the squared amplitude of x after U acts on the all-zero 98-qubit state. The target maximizes p\U over all 98-bit strings. Hardware shots sample q\Hx, the diagonal of the physical output density matrix.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1wrzZ4GBkilb4ehFlRS39uw.png In this notation U denotes the ideal circuit, x★ the target string, and ρH the physical output density matrix. The ideal peak probability and the experimentally observed distribution are distinct quantities. Statistical recovery therefore evaluates structure across the measured samples. Quantum hardware experiment Acquisition and statistical recovery The hardware runs produced 50 active P11 shots at a reported cost of 282.98 HQC and 200 P12 shots at 1,373.4 HQC. The source circuits, submitted artifacts, job records, raw results, and corrected datasets are preserved in the repository. Result framing needed repair before decoding. P11’s initial reconstruction contained 51 records, including one duplicated frame. P12 contained five overlapping frame replicas, producing 205 diagnostic records before repair. The final analyses use all 50 and 200 valid shots respectively. The repairs follow the provider’s output structure, before any candidate is scored. !Hardware shot counts over the full range of 0 to 98 bit differences from the accepted answer. P11 has one exact match out of 50. P12 has three out of 200. Most observations are farther away. Nonzero distances are grouped into five-bit bins.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1CtjsAbn456kLl09xrUhDfw.png Figure 1. The complete corrected hardware datasets. Distances are computed against the accepted answers after recovery. The broad tail can reflect both ideal off-peak mass and hardware noise. Hamming distance measures the number of differing bit positions. It quantifies local agreement among observations whose complete strings are distinct. A group of nearby outcomes can retain evidence of a common center even when that center has low observed multiplicity. The weighted observed medoid considers each observed string as a possible center and sums its Hamming distances to the whole dataset. Repeated strings receive their observed multiplicity cy. The candidate with the smallest total distance is selected. Cluster consensus first identifies a group C of mutually close observations, then votes on each bit within that group. The formulas below make the difference explicit. Sobs is the set of distinct observed strings, while cy records how often each occurred. !Hamming distance sums unequal bit positions. The observed medoid minimizes count-weighted total Hamming distance over observed candidates. Cluster consensus chooses one at a bit when its weighted count exceeds half of the selected cluster’s total weight, with zero on a tie.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1X0JKc6TvC3yweLPEX9UWQ.png The restriction to observed candidates matters. If the Hamming-distance objective were minimized over every possible string, each bit could be chosen independently, giving a whole-dataset majority vote. Restricting the center to an actual shot preserves a complete bit pattern that the device produced. That constraint can help when independent bit votes combine fragments from different parts of the distribution. The deterministic cluster decoder uses average-linkage clustering of normalized Hamming distances, with a cut at 0.15, then selects the cluster with the greatest shot weight. In the reproduced analysis the selected cluster contains seven shots for each circuit, including repeated observations. The cluster’s mean distance to its consensus is about 3.57 bits for P11 and 4.71 for P12. !A bit-by-bit comparison with the accepted answers. Whole-dataset majority differs at two P11 positions and thirteen P12 positions. The observed medoid and cluster consensus agree at all 98 positions for both circuits.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1XPNHrfSfWdFQK4FzX3boXQ.png Figure 2. Coral cells identify the bits missed by whole-dataset majority. Both the observed medoid and the cluster consensus recover all 98 accepted bits. The observed decoder performance is consistent with local concentration around the accepted strings. Each accepted answer was present and minimized the weighted-medoid objective over the observed candidates. The selected cluster also supported the same bitwise consensus. Whole-dataset majority differed from the accepted answers at two P11 positions and thirteen P12 positions. All P11 strings tied in frequency, whereas the accepted P12 string was the unique frequency mode. The resulting candidates were checked externally by the portal. Both hardware recovery submissions were subsequently verified in the Quantum Advantage Tracker. The measurements and their decoding establish successful answer recovery for these instances. P11 hardware recordhttps://github.com/quantum-advantage-tracker/quantum-advantage-tracker.github.io/issues/246 · P12 hardware recordhttps://github.com/quantum-advantage-tracker/quantum-advantage-tracker.github.io/issues/247 Classical structural reduction Inverse-pair identification and wire permutations The published P11 and P12 files contain 1,999 and 2,457 atomic two-qubit units. Each parsed unit contains a controlled-Z gate and its surrounding one-qubit rotations. Much of the length comes from an obfuscated middle placed between a prefix R and a suffix P. The classical solver examines the single-qubit rotations between consecutive controlled-Z gates. It fingerprints these rotations up to global phase, looking for a rotation A that later reappears as an inverse B. Such a pair would cancel if brought together. Several surviving inverse pairs reveal a larger mirrored arrangement of gates. The circuit has nested blocks, and a mirror can connect different wire labels. The solver therefore uses inverse-pair anchors to infer a consistent wire permutation through each block. The recorded runs find 419 inverse-pair anchors for P11 and 569 for P12. Composing the inferred maps yields a permutation Π for the middle. !A gate B approximately equal to A dagger up to phase approximately cancels A. Writing the full circuit as P M R, the solver approximates M by a wire permutation Pi and uses P Pi R as its reduced model.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1ML5AWroBRxaKualJueblmQ.png In this equation operations act from right to left. The input passes through R, then M, then P. A wire permutation can be absorbed into the labels of the suffix tensors, so the tensor network can be assembled without simulating a long sequence of explicit swap gates. The approximation sign is essential. Residual operations survive the obfuscation. Inferring a permutation gives a reduced model whose predictions must be evaluated. Its probability calculations describe that model. !Bars show the size of each published circuit and its inferred reduced core. P11 goes from 1,999 to 284 atomic two-qubit units, including one boundary move. P12 goes from 2,457 to 279, including two boundary moves.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1gCK0uQdlmDyryWw3PIbbdg.png Figure 3. Counts are taken from the recorded section boundaries and accepted frontier moves. They describe atomic two-qubit units in the QASM-based models. Tensor-network evaluation of the reduced model The primary reduction in classical cost arises from structural simplification before tensor contraction. Tensor-network contraction sums shared indices in a chosen order. Its cost is governed by the intermediate tensor sizes along that order. Removing the long mirrored middle leaves a shallow network with manageable intermediates for these instances. The solver then computes each output bit’s expectation of the Pauli-Z operator. A positive expectation favors zero, and a negative expectation favors one. The one-bit probabilities follow directly from that expectation. Combining the preferred bits gives a candidate whose amplitude is contracted separately. !The core expectation z\j is the all-zero-state expectation of U\core dagger Z\j U\core. The marginal probabilities of zero and one are 1+z\j/2 and 1-z\j/2. A candidate chooses one when z\j is nonpositive and is scored by its squared core amplitude.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/185a844MAat4JrvKA4MQO5Q.png Marginal evaluation provides an initial candidate without materializing the complete state vector. Joint correlations require a further check, since coordinate-wise marginal maximization need not identify the global probability mode. Boundary refinement Some obfuscation patches cross the inferred boundary between the prefix and the middle. Leaving the wrong frontier gate outside the core can weaken a marginal or change the candidate. Boundary repair tests adding accessible frontier gates to the retained model and scores the resulting candidates. In the recorded deterministic reproduction, the search chooses the best trial that improves the current candidate probability by at least 30%. It retains gate 59 for P11, and gates 60 then 64 for P12. This produces final models with 284 and 279 two-qubit units respectively. The upstream v2 implementation uses a different deterministic selection rule and reaches the same moves on these instances. !Candidate probability in the reduced core increases from 12.79 to 30.29 percent after gate 59 for P11. For P12 it increases from 0.52 to 5.42 and then 23.66 percent after gates 60 and 64.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1dh1yiqJctKFPxizKaLnwJQ.png Figure 4. Boundary repair changes the model and may change its candidate. The displayed probabilities belong to the core at each stage. The probability is a model-selection objective. It helped the search choose a useful boundary on P11 and P12. The repair procedure was developed after an initial P12 result missed the accepted answer by four bits. Runtime execution uses the QASM, with the published-answer comparison performed afterwards. Reuse of exact marginal evaluations Boundary search evaluates several very similar circuits. Recomputing every one-bit expectation from scratch repeats much of the same work. The second speed gain comes from recognizing which calculations remain identical across trials. Trace an output bit backward through the gates that can affect its Z expectation. These gates form its backward causal cone. Unitaries outside that cone cancel between the forward and conjugate networks in the expectation calculation. For fixed input and fixed gate matrices, an unchanged ordered cone gives exactly the same marginal. !K\j is the ordered sequence of gates in the backward causal cone of Z\j. For fixed inputs and gate matrices, identical ordered cones in two trial circuits imply identical z\j expectations.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1D6KYcn5qM4xavpONDSK6oQ.png The evaluator caches the marginal under that cone signature. It also reuses a contraction path when the ordered connectivity, index dimensions, and requested output match. Path reuse saves the search for a contraction order. The tensor values are still contracted for the current trial whenever a fresh expectation is needed. !The same search without caches takes 50.3 seconds for P11 and 86.3 for P12. With caches it takes 17.1 and 27.9 seconds. Marginal reuse is 78.1 and 82.8 percent respectively.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1xs8SPN1sPBaw8JiU9PMoiw.png Figure 5. The same deterministic search, measured once per mode on a MacBook M3 Pro. Times cover solving and exclude imports, certification, and the additional cache-validation contractions. For P11, sixteen core evaluations request 1,568 marginals, of which only 343 require a fresh contraction. For P12, thirty-two evaluations request 3,136, of which only 539 are new. Those counts explain the 78.1% and 82.8% reuse. In the recorded local comparison, solve time falls from 50.3 to 17.1 seconds for P11 and from 86.3 to 27.9 seconds for P12, giving 2.94× and 3.09× speedups. Independently recomputed final marginals agree with the cached results. Numerical certification of the reduced-core mode A final numerical certificate addresses the joint-probability question. Any competitor y that differs from the candidate at bit j has probability at most the marginal probability of that opposite bit. If that marginal is already smaller than the candidate’s complete probability, every competitor with that difference is eliminated at once. !If y differs from the candidate at bit j, its core probability is bounded by the opposite-bit marginal. When that marginal is smaller than the candidate probability, y cannot win.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/proxy/1LPV9S-ombzwwG1FCpwEtEQ.png Only differences on the remaining ambiguous wires need explicit amplitude checks. P11 has one such wire, leaving one competing string. P12 has five, leaving 31. The calculation certifies a unique global mode of each reduced core to a numerical tolerance of 10⁻¹⁰. The final candidate probabilities are approximately 0.302893 and 0.236559, and both recovered strings match all 98 bits of the corresponding accepted hardware answer. The structural approximation limits what follows from this certificate. It certifies the reduced model’s mode. Establishing an equally strong statement about the full obfuscated circuit would also require control of the operations discarded by that approximation. Recovered peak strings Quantum decoding and classical recovery produced identical 98-bit outputs for each instance. The canonical convention places qubit 0 at the left and qubit 97 at the right. For readability, each string is displayed below as two consecutive 49-bit lines. Concatenating the lines from top to bottom reconstructs the complete string. P11 peak 1010111011101001111110001011001110101110101111100 1010101101100001110101110010000010100001001100000 The P11 string occurred once among 50 corrected hardware shots, giving an empirical exact-match frequency of 2.0%. Both the weighted observed medoid and cluster consensus recovered this output. The recovered mode has probability 0.302893357 in the classical reduced model. P11 classical result recordhttps://github.com/MonitSharma/peakedcircuits/blob/10949ce/classicalsimulations/p11p12/results/P11.json P12 peak 1010001111001010011100010001110011000101111101110 0111001010110101011001001000000101000100000111100 The P12 string occurred 3 times among 200 corrected hardware shots, giving an empirical exact-match frequency of 1.5%. Both the weighted observed medoid and cluster consensus recovered this output. The recovered mode has probability 0.236559451 in the classical reduced model. P12 classical result recordhttps://github.com/MonitSharma/peakedcircuits/blob/10949ce/classicalsimulations/p11p12/results/P12.json The empirical hardware frequencies and the contracted core probabilities refer to different distributions. The former are measured proportions from finite physical-device datasets. The latter are numerical evaluations of the inferred reduced models. Their agreement on the recovered strings supplies a common verification endpoint while preserving the separate scope of each probability estimate. Interpretation and benchmark implications These results illustrate the dual role of peaked circuits. They permit an explicit answer-recovery endpoint for hardware evaluation, and they expose the strength of the classical methods applied to a specified circuit family. For P11 and P12, successful classical recovery is explained by surviving inverse fragments, recoverable wire mappings, and tractable reduced networks. The observed speed therefore depends on identifiable properties of these constructions. Assessing quantum advantage requires comparison with classical methods that exploit this structure. General complexity arguments about circuit families do not establish the difficulty of a particular released instance. The present records support reproducible hardware recovery and a detailed classical explanation of the same outputs, providing evidence for the continued refinement of verifiable benchmarks. Provenance and implementation Dylan Neve’s qsim-lab proposed the structural reduction and classical recovery method, with original VM runtimes of 89 seconds for P11 and 182 seconds for P12. The tracker submission credits Dylan Neve and Claude Anthropic. I reproduced the method and improved its evaluation loop with exact marginal caching, compatible contraction-path reuse, stable trial ordering, and reuse of an accepted trial. The reproduction also includes the reduced-core certificate described above. The cache changes and selection rule together improved the local implementation, and qsim-lab subsequently adopted my cached evaluator in its v2 solver. The issue discussion records that adoption and a separate same-VM comparison. P11 classical submissionhttps://github.com/quantum-advantage-tracker/quantum-advantage-tracker.github.io/issues/251 · P12 classical submission and implementation discussionhttps://github.com/quantum-advantage-tracker/quantum-advantage-tracker.github.io/issues/252 The timings in Figure 5 compare the same search with its caches off and on, using the local benchmark records. The original VM timings belong to a different environment. The tracker has verified the classical P11 submission, and its reviewer reproduced both P12 solver versions in the open P12 issue. The hardware and classical records answer complementary questions. The hardware run shows what could be recovered from its actual measurements. The classical analysis identifies the surviving construction that made these particular files tractable. The repository contains the inputs and intermediate records behind both results. title: The Hidden Arithmetic Behind Quantum Finance
excerpt: How compact state and language-model-assisted design reduced the arithmetic behind two complex financial contracts.
text: How compact state and language-model-assisted design reduced the arithmetic behind two complex financial contracts. !Workflow from contract rules and encoded market shocks to compact state, temporary payoff arithmetic and a payoff angle. A language model proposes circuit designs; tools evaluate them; final candidates undergo separate validation. Matched TQ reductions are 2.39-fold for the autocallable and 4.84-fold for TARF. The HHL angle circuit has a 14.1 percent lower TQ than Gu et al.’s published point, using eleven more logical qubits.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1yLpbrAD542WKLgveCQnwXA.png Our approach at a glance: fix the contract, explore compact circuit designs, then assess their cost and correctness separately. The savings shown cover arithmetic components, not a complete pricing system. A financial contract can fit on a few pages and still be surprisingly expensive to calculate. Its payment might depend on three assets, a barrier crossed months ago, and whether the contract should have ended early. Today’s price alone does not tell you what the investor receives. Now imagine evaluating those rules across a large collection of possible futures. That is the work hiding inside many derivative-pricing problems. The final answer is an average; producing each term in that average can be the difficult part. In our new paper, we study this arithmetic inside quantum pricing. We use a language model to help design smaller circuits, and find 2.39× and 4.84× reductions in a logical resource metric for two fixed finance benchmarks. We also improve the gate–qubit product of an HHL angle circuit reported by Gu et al.https://arxiv.org/html/2610.22367v1 The idea connecting these results is quite practical: reconsider what the circuit needs to remember. Before getting to the circuits, though, it helps to understand the contracts they are trying to calculate. A contract that can end before maturity An autocallable is a structured contract that can terminate automatically on a scheduled observation date if its underlying assets meet a specified condition. The payment depends on the contract’s rules, and the possibility of an early exit changes the paths we need to track. Our benchmark is a three-asset, worst-of autocallable. “Worst-of” means that the weakest-performing asset matters. Imagine each asset starts at a relative price of 100. At a call date, all three must be at least 110 for the early-payment condition to be met. Prices of 112, 115 and 111 meet it; prices of 112, 115 and 109 do not. There is also a downside barrier at 70. If any asset falls below it at a monitoring date, that event can activate a terminal loss if the contract survives without being called and the worst asset finishes below its starting level. A later recovery does not erase the earlier barrier event. So the computation has to remember more than the latest prices. It needs to know whether a call has occurred and whether the downside barrier has been breached. Our benchmark has 20 monitoring dates and five scheduled call dates. These are fixed research rules, not a calibrated market product. A contract with a running target A target accrual redemption forward, or TARF, has a different kind of memory. It makes a sequence of payments and keeps a running total. Once that total reaches a target, the contract ends. A separate knockout condition can end it earlier. In our 26-date benchmark, the underlying starts at 20 and the accrual target is 5. Prices between 20 and the knockout level of 30 generate positive payments; prices from 15 up to 20 generate none; below 15, the payment is negative, with twice the exposure to the difference from 20. Reaching 30 knocks the contract out before that date’s payment. The target clips the last payment. If 3 has already accrued and the next eligible payment would be 4, the contract pays only 2 and stops at 5. Negative payments, meanwhile, reduce the running total. They are not silently replaced with zero. This gives us a second path-dependent problem. The same current asset price can lead to different remaining payments depending on what has already accrued and whether the contract is still alive. Why a quantum algorithm still has to do the bookkeeping To price either contract under a chosen model, we average its discounted payments over possible market paths. Classical Monte Carlo does this by sampling paths, evaluating the payments and averaging them. Quantum amplitude estimation offers a better dependence on the desired precision in the ideal query model: it can use quadratically fewer calls to a payoff calculation than Monte Carlo. But every call needs an actual implementation of the contract rules. Chakrabarti et al.https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2021-06-01-463/ studied the resources required for quantum pricing with autocallable and TARF benchmarks, providing the setting we build on. Those calls have an extra constraint. In ordinary software, we can overwrite temporary values. A coherent quantum circuit must clear its workspace correctly so that leftover information does not interfere with the larger computation. Updating a price, testing a barrier, and undoing temporary calculations can all cost gates and qubits. Our question is about that work: can we make the reversible payoff arithmetic cheaper while understanding the approximation errors it introduces? Keep the running total, reconstruct the detail Think about tracking your spending. If the next question only needs your total, you probably keep a running sum. You do not rebuild it from every receipt each time. You retain extra details when another rule needs them. The market model in our benchmarks offers a similar opportunity. Each random shock is selected by a five-bit integer index. The shock grid is equally spaced, the model coefficients are fixed, and the observation dates are uniformly spaced. Together, these choices mean that current log-returns can be reconstructed from cumulative sums of the indices. For the autocallable, the factor-sum design keeps three exact 10-bit market-state counters, alongside the contract’s history. It reconstructs weighted quantities temporarily when a barrier decision or terminal payoff needs them. For TARF, one index sum, accrual tracking and date-dependent lookup tables avoid much of the repeated price reconstruction. The contract memory stays. A sum describing the current market state cannot tell us whether an earlier barrier was crossed or how much has already been paid. What changes is the amount of wide arithmetic state carried between dates. At the end, the arithmetic produces a payoff angle: a number that a later quantum rotation can use to encode the payment. We study the arithmetic after the market inputs have been loaded and before that rotation and the estimation algorithm. The language model proposes; the circuit has to pass the checks Our design process follows the evaluator-guided approach of Gu et al.https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22367 A language model proposes circuit programs, tools evaluate them, and feedback guides revisions. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to help explore representations, write circuit-building code and refine implementations. The useful output is a program we can inspect and measure. Separate tools recount its resources and check its behavior. The authors set the tasks and rules and interpret the results. A convincing explanation from the model does not establish that the circuit is correct. This was an assisted design process. Early runs included human hints and full-repository access, some early exact model identifiers are unavailable, and the six retained TARF programs share one design lineage. These details matter when deciding what the results say about the circuits and what they say about the reliability of the search method. Reading the resource plots The plots below have two axes: Toffoli-equivalent gate count on the horizontal axis and peak live logical qubits on the vertical axis. Moving left means less arithmetic work; moving down means less workspace. The gate axis is logarithmic, so equal horizontal distances represent equal ratios. We combine the two resources into TQ = Toffoli-equivalent count × peak logical qubits. The dashed curves join designs with the same product. A Pareto frontier captures another useful idea: designs for which improving one resource requires giving up something in the other. A resource frontier does not, by itself, rank financial accuracy. !Three resource tradeoff panels from the paper. In the original autocallable, factor-sum uses 7,551 Toffoli-equivalent gates and 518 logical qubits versus 16,810 and 556 for the reference, reducing TQ 2.39-fold. TARF separates a 199.5-fold representation change from a subsequent 4.84-fold search improvement. In the second autocallable setting, generic transfer loses its advantage and fresh lattice-form designs recover smaller savings. Hollow circles denote screening-only evidence.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1CnL8GiUEVz3VNSFjxXWYJQ.png Finance resource plots from the paper. Horizontal: Toffoli-equivalent gates; vertical: peak live logical qubits. Hollow search circles have empirical screening only; filled search circles have held-out validation. R compares the named reference product with the candidate product. The frontiers rank resources, not accuracy. The bottom panel shows the second parameter setting discussed below. For the autocallable, the log-return reference uses 16,810 Toffoli-equivalent gates and 556 logical qubits. The factor-sum circuit uses 7,551 and 518. That lowers the product from 9,346,360 to 3,911,418: a 2.39× reduction, or about 58%. For TARF, the lookup reference uses 28,428 gates and 384 qubits. The final windowed circuit uses 8,381 and 269. Its product falls from 10,916,352 to 2,254,489: a 4.84× reduction, or about 79%. The two arrows in the TARF plot tell different stories. Moving from the expensive price-space reconstruction to the lookup reference gives a roughly 199.5× representation saving. The 4.84× improvement then starts from that already cheaper lookup reference. Keeping those comparisons separate makes it clear where the gains come from. These are logical arithmetic costs. The counts exclude market-distribution loading, payoff rotations, amplitude estimation and physical error correction. They give us better components to work with; establishing a complete pricing advantage requires the rest of the system too. An HHL improvement, with a visible tradeoff We also used a separate arithmetic calibration from HHL, the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd algorithm for linear systemshttps://arxiv.org/abs/0811.3171. Here the task is to calculate a rotation angle from an encoded input. It is a compact way to test numerical circuit design outside the two financial contracts. For this angle task, the best published point in Gu et al.’s resource tablehttps://arxiv.org/html/2610.22367v1 uses 1,348 Toffoli gates and 115 qubits, giving a product of 155,020. Our Booth-polynomial circuit uses 1,057 gates and 126 qubits, giving 133,182. That is a 14.1% lower product. !HHL angle resource plot with logarithmic Toffoli gate axis and peak logical-qubit axis. Gu et al.’s orange diamond is at 1,348 gates and 115 qubits. Our filled teal Booth-polynomial point is at 1,057 gates and 126 qubits, with a 14.1 percent lower product but eleven more qubits. The HRS reconstruction and dyadic reference are also shown. Hollow teal points have screening evidence only.https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1qccRP57Vbsn7FMHXM-oZw.png The paper’s HHL angle-calibration plot. Our Booth-polynomial point is left of and above Gu et al.’s orange diamond: fewer Toffoli gates, eleven more logical qubits, and a 14.1% lower product. Hollow teal points have screening evidence only. The dashed curves have equal TQ; the frontier ranks resources, not accuracy. This comparison covers the angle component. The geometry is useful here. Our point moves left but also slightly up: it uses fewer gates and more qubits. It improves the product without dominating Gu et al.’s point on both axes. Which design is preferable can depend on how a larger implementation values work and memory. The HHL circuit’s integer action has exact all-input logical checks. A separate exhaustive comparison over 2,031,616 inputs finds a maximum angle error of about 9.72 × 10⁻⁸ radians, below the 10⁻⁷ target. That accuracy comparison is numerical, without a certified enclosure. The resource improvement belongs to this angle task, not to a complete implementation of HHL. A million successful tests can still miss the interesting cases The most important verification lesson is that two questions need different answers. Does the circuit execute its intended integer calculation correctly? And does that calculation approximate the financial payment closely enough? For the factor-sum autocallable, we prove the coherent integer action for every encoded input, every incoming output-accumulator value and every measurement record, including clean workspace and cancellation of unwanted phases. The proof uses computational certificates under the stated ideal circuit semantics. That calculation still approximates the contract. Rounded coefficients can shift a barrier decision, some early barrier tests are omitted, and finite-width terminal arithmetic can wrap. Executing the integer specification perfectly does not remove those financial errors. The factor-sum circuit had zero violations in a million-path independent high-precision study and in a separate million-path task-reference holdout. Yet 241 of 900 deliberately selected stress paths exceed the tolerance. Those paths were chosen to expose problems; their failure fraction is not a loading-law frequency. A separate lattice calculation follows probability through states that recombine, allowing rare cases to be assessed more directly. Under the benchmark’s specified discrete loading law, it numerically estimates an angle-tolerance-violation probability of about 6.248 × 10⁻⁸, roughly one in sixteen million, and evaluates the pricing bias. The angle tolerance is 10⁻⁵ radians. This is a numerical estimate with bounded omitted probability mass, not a fully certified numerical interval covering all rounding and function-evaluation errors. It is also a result for the declared discrete model. The final TARF circuit passed its separate million-path reference studies, but retains selected counterexamples and does not have the same all-input coherent-action proof. The result that did not travel The bottom panel of the finance plot is a useful check on the enthusiasm. When we changed the autocallable’s volatility and correlation parameters, a generic adaptation of the factor-sum approach became 5.58 times more expensive in TQ than the transferred log-return reference. The original favorable structure did not automatically survive the change. Fresh bounded search found a shift-add lattice-form design with a 1.35× lower product than that reference. That is a recovery at one further setting. It also shows why the original savings should not be assumed to extend to arbitrary contracts, precisions or model parameters. What I hope this makes easier to see Quantum finance is often introduced through the number of samples an algorithm can save. This work looks inside one of those calls, where representations, temporary values and contract memory determine how expensive the arithmetic becomes. A language model helped us explore those choices. Resource recounts, logical verification and financial-error analysis made the resulting circuits assessable. The next step is to connect components like these to complete pricing implementations and understand how the tradeoffs change as the problems grow. For me, the useful design lesson is the running total: keep the information the next step needs, reconstruct the detail when required, and be precise about what gets forgotten. That is a good question to ask of a quantum circuit — and a productive place to involve a language model. title: From 5,329 Layers to 111: How I Optimized a Quantum Phase Oracle
excerpt: Class codes, quantum interference, and the scheduling problem hidden between compute and uncompute
text: Class codes, quantum interference, and the scheduling problem hidden between compute and uncompute !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/554/1yYxUYw8lVzQmOngkiUK7Zw.jpeg My final circuit for the Classiq Quantum Circuit Challenge had depth 111, using 18 qubits, 557 CX gates, and 423 U3 gates. The supplied baseline had depth 5,329. That is a 48.0-fold reduction in depth, or about 97.9% fewer layers. The result came from changing the representation of the problem, then optimizing the interfaces between the resulting circuit stages. The last few layers required more than finding a shorter encoder or removing another gate: they required arranging for the right information to arrive on the right wire at the right time. The challenge is now over. Classiq’s published recaphttps://www.classiq.io/insights/wrapping-up-the-classiq-quantum-circuit-challenge reports a best depth of 95, so 111 is not the best known result. It is my verified submission, and this article explains the construction and the experiments that led to it. The recap also gives several directions for continuing the optimization after the competition. The task: a picture encoded as phase The input was a pair of six-bit coordinates, x and y, identifying one of the 4,096 pixels in a 64 × 64 image of the Classiq logo. The circuit had to change the sign of a basis state exactly when its pixel belonged to the logo: |x, y⟩ |000000⟩ → expiφ −1^fx,y |x, y⟩ |000000⟩ The global phase φ could be arbitrary, but it had to be the same for every input. The coordinates had to survive unchanged, and all six auxiliary qubits had to return to zero. Those requirements make the operation usable on a coherent superposition, as a phase oracle in a larger quantum algorithm. The predicate was the union of a square, a horizontal bar, and two disks: def logox, y: return 2 <= x <= 26 and 29 <= y <= 53 or 26 <= x <= 49 and 39 <= y <= 43 or x - 55\\2 + y - 41\\2 <= 42 or x - 40\\2 + y - 19\\2 <= 72 There are 1,097 marked pixels. A classical program can evaluate that expression directly. A reversible quantum circuit has to implement the sign coherently while cleaning up its workspace. The scoring model mattered throughout the project. Every U3 or CX gate occupied one layer; gates on disjoint wires could run together; connectivity was all-to-all. Depth was the primary objective and CX count broke ties. This was an abstract circuit synthesis benchmark. Depth 111 is not a claim about execution time or fidelity on a particular physical processor. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/174Z9JHETDxlgS76RUlWPg.png Figure 1. Target predicate, repeated row and column patterns, and phase-polynomial sizes. The image contains much less independent information than a general 12-bit truth table. Why my first circuits were still too deep Several plausible representations produced working circuits without producing a sufficiently shallow one. Direct Boolean synthesis, geometry-based multiplexers, comparator identities, and distributed lookup all appeared in the exploration. The direct phase representation was particularly revealing. A Boolean predicate can be expanded in bit parities, with phase rotations implementing the coefficients. Here, all 4,095 nonconstant parities of the original twelve coordinate bits have nonzero coefficients. Optimizing the traversal of that dense expansion leaves a very large circuit. My intermediate results show how much the architecture changed: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1ldgx9FeGTFjA5RXlodg7og.png Selected verified milestones. The final submission is highlighted: depth 111, 557 CX gates. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1XLYLUePgccXy5Pt3u7j2fA.png Optimization history from the repository. Left: best verified depth on a log scale; the 5,329-layer baseline is not plotted. Right: depth versus CX count near the final circuits, with 111 / 557 highlighted. These are selected verified milestones, rather than every search result. The progression also illustrates why fewer CX gates did not always mean lower depth: a substitution could save gates while making a critical wire wait longer. Compressing the information before compiling it The important structural observation was that the logo has only 11 distinct column patterns and 11 distinct row patterns. If two x coordinates give the same column, no y coordinate can distinguish them through the predicate. They can share a column-class label. The same reasoning applies to rows. The phase decision can therefore be represented by a small class-pair table, provided the circuit also computes the coordinate-to-class mappings. Four bits are enough to distinguish eleven classes. But assigning class numbers from zero to ten would optimize a classical data structure, not necessarily the reversible implementation. The label assignment changes both the cost of computing the labels and the phase polynomial needed to combine them. I used four-bit codes of the form p, L: one raw coordinate parity p, plus a three-bit label L. For x, the parity was x₄ XOR x₅; for y, it was y₅. Labels were assigned to the combinations of parity and pattern class so the code still determined the correct class. The resulting x mapping reached 14 of the 16 code words; y reached 13. Together, only 182 of 256 eight-bit addresses were reachable. The other 74 addresses provided useful freedom. The oracle would never see them when the loaders began with clean ancillas, so their phase values could be selected to simplify the implementation. The best completion used a 63-term phase polynomial, compared with 4,095 nonconstant terms in the direct coordinate representation. The important cost was still the complete circuit. A beautifully sparse kernel could lose its advantage if its labels were expensive to compute. Loading labels through interference The final architecture was compute–phase–uncompute: coordinate loaders → phase kernel → inverse coordinate loaders The x and y loaders each worked on nine wires: six coordinate inputs and three ancillas. The middle kernel acted on the eight code wires. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1p2faYqEwACA2z0AJfLt4hA.png Figure 2. Compute–phase–uncompute with overlapping coordinate loaders and the central phase kernel. Individual wires can move into the kernel while other parts of a loader are still finishing. To compute a Boolean label bit L onto a clean target, I used interference. A Hadamard opened the target into two branches. A diagonal circuit added a relative phase of πL between those branches. A second Hadamard converted that relative phase into the computational-basis value L. For a fixed input, the essential identity is: H · diag1, −1^L · H |0⟩ = |L⟩ The diagonal circuit itself was built from CX gates and parity rotations. A CX changes which parity a wire carries; a rotation applies a phase when that wire holds the required parity. There was another useful freedom: a loader could introduce a phase depending only on its input coordinates. Its exact inverse later cancelled that phase. The loader therefore did not need to be a phase-perfect implementation of a standalone classical function, provided the complete sandwich remained correct. Let earlier labels help compute later ones Computing all three label bits independently was wasteful. Once the first label was available, later encoders could use it as another input. They only needed to be correct on combinations of the coordinates and first label that actually occurred. This conditional construction reduced the rotation support to 45 + 21 + 23 terms on x and 45 + 30 + 14 on y: 89 per side, down from roughly 170 in the earlier formulation. All three target frames could open in the first layer. Their computations overlapped, with only genuinely dependent rotations waiting for the earlier label to close. This change helped bring the complete circuit from depth 185 to 151. Choose the output basis too The outputs did not have to be the original three label bits themselves. Any suitable invertible combination could describe the same classes, if the kernel was changed consistently. One useful x basis was L₀, L₁, L₁ XOR L₂. This introduced a joint optimization: choose the labels, choose their output basis, and then synthesize both the loaders and kernel. Optimizing any one of those pieces in isolation missed opportunities in the others. The required phase is only defined modulo 2π A relative phase of π and a relative phase of 3π produce the same sign. More generally, a loader only needed phase πLx modulo 2π. I could add an integer multiple of 2π independently at each input without changing the label produced by interference. Those integer choices changed the Walsh coefficients of the phase function. Some choices removed rotations. For the six-bit angle representation used in the search, the constraints became a linear system modulo 64. I used Howell normal form to handle that arithmetic; ordinary Gaussian elimination over a field does not apply unchanged to a modulus that is a prime power. Saving one or two rotations sounds small. Near the final schedules, it could decide whether a label closed early enough for the kernel to fit. The real objective: when each wire becomes usable The most useful change in perspective was to stop treating a loader’s total depth as its score. Suppose a code wire is ready after r layers and the whole circuit must finish in T layers. In a symmetric compute–uncompute picture, the inverse loader needs its corresponding r layers at the end. The middle operations have a window: r + 1 ≤ kernel layer ≤ T − r At T = 111, a wire ready at layer 45 has only layers 46 through 66 available: 21 layers. A different wire ready earlier has more room. Those windows matter more than the moment the last gate anywhere in the loader finishes. The final design’s latest x and y code bits were ready at layers 43 and 45. The search tracked the entire vector of ready times because different code bits participate in different numbers of kernel operations. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/16STDgjP7CunTbQFhPqw86A.png Figure 3. Availability windows for the eight code wires in the depth-111 circuit. The latest labels leave the narrowest windows. Improving an already-early wire may do little for the total depth. A layer-synchronous beam search built CX matchings across the nine wires of each loader. It placed a rotation when a wire carried a required parity. A freeze action retired a wire once it held a completed code bit, but only when the remaining rotations were still representable using the other wires. The kernel search then worked within the wire-specific windows. It had to visit its required phase parities and restore an appropriate final basis for the unloaders. Why the timing model needed to match the assembled circuit The simple window formula explains the pressure, but the final implementation needed finer rules. A phase rotation adjacent to a closing Hadamard could fuse with it into one U3 gate. A diagonal rotation could sometimes move across a commuting boundary operation. But a wire could not host a rotation in the same layer as a CX using that wire. An optimistic timing model could therefore declare a candidate feasible even though its assembled U3/CX circuit was too deep. I replaced that approximation with an exact fused model and checked assembled schedules using a time-indexed mixed-integer program solved with HiGHS. The constraints placed each gate exactly once, prevented wire conflicts, and preserved the order of noncommuting operations. This provided a rigorous scheduling check within the specified gate list and commutation model. It did not prove a lower bound over every possible circuit implementing the oracle. From 115 to 111: change what closes onto the wire The final reductions used the boundary between phase loading and classical labels. If a target closes with a Hadamard and the first kernel operation is a CX into that target, commuting the CX through the Hadamard turns it into a CZ before the close. In the phase-loading frame, that CZ changes the relative sign and therefore changes which Boolean label emerges. This made it useful to load L₁ XOR L₀ rather than L₁, while changing the kernel’s starting basis to match. The logical class information stayed sufficient, but the kernel began from a more convenient set of parities. For one x-loader relabeling, two existing rotation angles changed and one rotation was added in an idle slot. The CX and Hadamard schedule stayed the same. Yet the new starting basis let the middle circuit fit at depth 114. Extending the relabeling to both coordinate registers gave 113. Making the y-parity target available earlier gave 112. For 111, I selected target functions with sparse rotation support and screened loader pairs against their exact kernel starting bases before spending the larger beam-search budget. The first complete depth-111 circuit used 561 CX gates. A lower-CX x loader and local resynthesis produced the final 557-CX circuit. The recorded reconstruction recipe uses an x-loader ready-time profile of 39 / 40 / 41 / 43, a kernel beam width of 12,000, and subsequent exact scheduling and three-qubit resynthesis. Saving gates without losing a layer Local optimization was useful, but its acceptance criterion had to be depth-aware. I used commutation-aware CX cancellation, fusion of neighbouring single-qubit gates, SAT searches for smaller parity-network windows, and numerical resynthesis of small three-qubit blocks. Numerical candidates were fitted and refined, then checked before insertion into the full circuit. At depth 115, roughly 280 exact substitutions with fewer CX gates were available, but each increased the depth to at least 116. That was a concrete reminder that minimizing gate count and minimizing latency are different problems. The final stage attribution was: - Stage: x loader · CX: 120 · U3: 91 - Stage: y loader · CX: 120 · U3: 90 - Stage: Phase kernel · CX: 79 · U3: 62 - Stage: x unloader · CX: 119 · U3: 91 - Stage: y unloader · CX: 119 · U3: 89 - Stage: Total · CX: 557 · U3: 423 Boundary fusion and local rewrites explain why the counts are not perfectly symmetric even though the architecture uses inverse loading operations. Counts are attributed using the recorded kernel windows. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/15GuIIwYhe1LymU1JOv-XyA.png Figure 4. Gate-level schedule of the final 18-qubit circuit: depth 111, 557 CX, and 423 U3. The circuit’s 980 gates fit into 111 layers through parallel execution and careful ordering. Verification was part of every claimed improvement A phase oracle can produce correct pixel values while still introducing unwanted relative phases. Checking only the Boolean predicate would miss that error. For each reported circuit, I propagated all 4,096 clean-ancilla basis inputs through the actual QASM. The check required the original coordinate state, clean ancillas, and the correct sign with one common global phase across every input. The original final-circuit verifier reported a largest numerical deviation of 5.57 × 10⁻¹⁴. The independent NumPy implementation reported about 6.66 × 10⁻¹⁴, consistent with different floating-point evaluation paths. Both passed. The QASM’s SHA-256 is recorded with its verification report so the result identifies an exact artifact. By linearity, agreement on every clean-ancilla basis input establishes the intended action on arbitrary superpositions of those inputs, within the numerical verification tolerance. It does not claim equivalent behaviour when the workspace starts in an arbitrary nonzero state. The lightweight reproduction command is: python scripts/verify\circuit.py submission/submission.qasm What the winning circuits suggest next Classiq’s recap provides a useful comparison with the approach I took. Its five published winning results were: - Depth: 95 · CX: 272 - Depth: 95 · CX: 410 - Depth: 106 · CX: 360 - Depth: 108 · CX: 500 - Depth: 109 · CX: 481 Results and architecture descriptions: Classiq challenge recaphttps://www.classiq.io/insights/wrapping-up-the-classiq-quantum-circuit-challenge. The geometry-based results motivate revisiting my earlier comparator experiments. An exact identity alone was insufficient in my work: its reversible encoders also needed to become cheaper. The joint-encoding result motivates testing a smaller interface. The recap does not supply its feature maps or synthesis code, so reconstructing a similar circuit remains a new experiment. The phase-loading results motivate extending my searches over encoder choices, phase corrections, and local substitutions. These are descriptions of possible research directions, not claims that I have reproduced the winning circuits. What depth 111 does — and does not — establish The depth-111 schedule contains a tight wire path: 45 loader layers, 21 kernel touches, and 45 unloader layers. My searches did not find a complete depth-110 construction. That says something about the explored gate lists and architectures; it does not establish 111 as an optimum. The published depth-95 results make the remaining room for improvement explicit. The lesson I take from this project is that representation, reversible computation, and scheduling need to be designed together. Repeated patterns simplified the information. Interference made the labels cheaper to compute. Unreachable addresses and modulo-2π freedom simplified phase functions. Wire-level timing made those savings useful in the complete circuit. The competition supplied a deadline. The remaining gap supplies a research question: which distinctions must the oracle retain, and how cheaply can a reversible circuit make them available? Code and technical details The repositoryhttps://github.com/MonitSharma/classiq-quantum-circuit-challenge includes the submitted QASM, verification reports, intermediate circuits, and reconstruction data. The technical reporthttps://github.com/MonitSharma/classiq-quantum-circuit-challenge/blob/main/docs/technical-report.md gives the derivation and scheduling details.
